strengths: Introduces a genuinely novel and underexplored problem formulation -- lifelong 3D head avatar modeling from unstructured, in-the-wild photo collections spanning decades -- which is a meaningful departure from the dominant momentary-capture paradigm in head avatar research.

The technical design is well-motivated and grounded in classical 3DMM principles (additive mean + basis combination), extended sensibly into a neural setting via the Dynamo module (dynamic basis pruning/blending) and DNA-2DGS (inverse-warping-based dynamic 2D Gaussian Splatting) that separately handles lifestage deformation and motion/expression warping.

Extensive experimentation: two evaluation protocols (1v1 and 1vN), comparisons against 8+ baselines spanning NeRF-based, 3DGS-based, generative, and one-shot avatar paradigms, plus mesh reconstruction comparisons, reenactment demos, and multiple ablations (Dynamo, hashgrid count, loss terms, residual embedding).

Contribution of a new large-scale dataset (TimeWalker-1.0, 40 identities, 2.7M frames) with thorough statistical characterization (age, ethnicity, headpose, brightness variance) and comparison to existing datasets, which could serve as a useful benchmark for the community.

Thoughtful supplementary explorations (large-scale pretraining for data augmentation/post-processing, 3D editing downstream application, lighting control) and an honest limitations/failure-case discussion (tongue/mouth artifacts, large-yaw degradation, incomplete lifelong span), along with a considered ethics statement given the use of real celebrity identities.
weaknesses: Evaluation protocol (holding out the last 10% of frames per lifestage) tests interpolation/held-out-frame reconstruction within already-observed lifestages rather than genuine generalization to unseen lifestages or extrapolated ages, which is the paper's central claim ("time traveling"); no quantitative evaluation isolates this age-extrapolation capability beyond qualitative figures.

Reliance solely on PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS (plus a late ArcFace ID-consistency comparison against only one baseline) is insufficient to substantiate the core claim of long-horizon identity preservation and perceptually convincing age/appearance disentanglement; no user study is included despite the strongly perceptual nature of the claims (realism, identity consistency across decades).

Main paper experiments use only 5 of the 40 dataset identities, and several key comparisons (e.g., against PAV) rely on a self-reimplementation (INSTA++) rather than the original method, since PAV is not open-sourced -- this introduces potential bias into the strongest related-work comparison.

The method requires per-identity training (a personalized model per person), which, combined with reliance on noisy FLAME fits from uncontrolled internet imagery, limits practical scalability and reproducibility; dataset release is stated as a future non-commercial release rather than available now, so full reproducibility cannot be currently verified.

Novel component Dynamo is a relatively simple thresholded pruning heuristic on blending weights; ablations show only modest gains over a well-chosen fixed hashgrid count, somewhat tempering the claimed significance of "dynamic" basis discovery.

Practical limitations remain notable relative to the ambitious framing: large-yaw view synthesis degrades beyond 45°, unseen mouth interior/tongue is not modeled, exaggerated expressions are under-represented, and the lifelong span covered per identity is still partial (not infancy-to-old-age), which somewhat undercuts the "comprehensive lifelong" framing in the abstract/title.

Ethical concerns around using real celebrities' likenesses (including movie footage) for building animatable avatars are acknowledged but not deeply resolved beyond a non-commercial license pledge, which is a nontrivial issue for a dataset intended for community release.
